notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0553.tlg001.1st1K-gr: The text has run-together and garbled words (ὑπομένωονἀκούειν is read as ὑπομένων ἀκούειν). Near the end, μ’ ἐξ ἁπλῶν is doubtful: it is rendered 'and from simple [principles]'; if it stands for μὴ ἐξ ἁπλῶν, the sense is 'not from bare [statements]'.

nodes.text: Often I have been urged to set out on the present undertaking, and have held back, 'yielding neither to sloth nor to thoughtlessness of mind', as the poet says, but above all awed by the grandeur and the number of the principles it contains, and fearing the objections of men who say what they say either because they are convinced that there is no divination and no providence of the gods, or else because they are providing themselves with exercises and pastimes. But now the present need, pressing because of its usefulness not only to ourselves but also to the men who will come after us, has urged me not to delay or put it off, but to write down whatever I have an understanding of, an understanding I acquired through experience. And I think that I shall gain two things from such a work: that I shall stand against those who try to do away with divination itself and its kinds, both without giving offence and with no ordinary argument, bringing into the open my experience and the testimony of the outcomes, which would be enough to withstand all men; and further, that for those who make use of divination but, because they have not met with accurate accounts of these matters, have gone astray and are now in danger of despising it and falling away from it, I shall establish a saving cure in place of their error. For nearly all those a little older than ourselves, wishing to win a reputation as writers, and thinking that they would become famous by this alone, if they left behind treatises on the interpretation of dreams, have made copies of one another, or have explained badly what was well said by the ancients and added many untrue things to a few of the ancients'; for they wrote not from experience but improvising, each as he was moved about any given thing; and some had read all the books of the ancients, others not all, for some, being rare through their age and corrupted, escaped their notice. But I, for my part, on the one hand, there is no book of dream interpretation that I have not acquired, since I have great zeal for this; on the other hand, though the diviners in the marketplace are greatly slandered, whom those who put on solemn faces and raise their eyebrows call beggars and sorcerers and buffoons, I despised the slander and for many years kept company with them, both in Greece, in its cities and at its festivals, and in Asia and in Italy and in the largest and most populous of the islands, patiently listening to old dreams and their outcomes; for there was no other way to get practice in these matters. From this it has come about that I have, in abundance, more to say about each thing than one might expect, and so as, speaking the very truth, not to talk idly; and, for whatever I mention, to give proofs that are clear and easily grasped by all, and from simple [principles], unless something should be so plain that I consider an explanation of it superfluous.

Of those called trustworthy, whom one must believe and obey when they say something in a dream, I say that the first are the gods; for lying is foreign to a god. Next come priests; for they have received from men the same honour as the gods. Then kings and rulers; for 'what holds power has the might of a god'. Then parents and teachers; for these too are like gods, the former bringing [us] into life, the latter teaching how one ought to use life. Then seers, but of seers only those who are not cheats or false seers. For whatever Pythagorists, physiognomists, diviners by knucklebones, by cheese and by sieves, readers of forms, readers of palms, diviners by basins and diviners by the dead may say, one must consider it all false and baseless; for their arts are of that kind, and they themselves know not even a little of divination, but by bewitching and deceiving they strip bare those who come to them. It remains, then, that the only true things are those said by sacrificers, augurs, star-gazers, interpreters of portents, interpreters of dreams and inspectors of livers. As for the mathematicians who cast nativities, let us examine them. The dead too are among the trustworthy, since they always speak the truth; for liars deceive for these two reasons, either because they hope for something or because they are afraid; but those who neither hope for anything nor fear naturally speak the truth. And the dead above all are of this kind. Again, little children speak the truth; for they do not yet know how to lie and deceive. So do the very old; for they show their trustworthiness through their age. And dumb animals always speak the truth, because they have no art of speech. All the rest, not to go through them one by one, lie in whatever they say, except those who are trustworthy in everyday life and upright in character. Theatre people and those who go up on the stage are, simply because of their play-acting, untrustworthy to everyone; so are sophists, paupers, *galloi* [castrated priests of Cybele], the castrated and eunuchs; for these, even when they say nothing, show that hopes are false, because by nature they are counted neither among men nor among women. One must therefore believe the trustworthy when they speak about all other matters as well.
